modern_osis:
Micah — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)

God raised up Micah to support Isaiah and confirm his prophecies.

Micah called the people to repentance through warnings of coming judgment and promises of mercy.

Micah chapter 5 contains an especially remarkable summary of prophecies concerning the Messiah.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe wrath of God against Israel.1–7Also against Jerusalem and other cities, Their precautions vain.8–16
God's wrath against Israel (verses 1–7)

The whole earth and everything within it is summoned to hear the prophet.

God's holy temple cannot protect people who profess to worship him while living hypocritically.

Neither the great and powerful, pictured by mountains, nor ordinary people, pictured by valleys, can protect themselves or their land from divine judgment.

God does not overlook sin among those who claim to belong to him.

Indeed, their sins especially offend him because they bring disgrace upon his name.

When we suffer the consequences of wrongdoing, it is wise to examine what particular sin has caused us to suffer.

People and places held in the greatest honor can be especially exposed to spiritual diseases.

The sins of leaders and rulers will be punished severely.

The judgment will correspond to the sin.

What the people sacrificed to their idols will never make them prosperous or truly help them.

Wealth gained through one sinful desire is often consumed by another.

Jerusalem and the other cities cannot escape (verses 8–16)

Micah grieved over Israel's desperate condition.

But the people should not announce it in Gath, giving enjoyment to those who delight in God's people's sins or suffering.

The prophet spoke of lying in the dust as a mourner.

Let every house in Jerusalem become a house of Aphrah, meaning “house of dust” in Henry's explanation.

When God humbles us to the dust, it is right for us to humble ourselves beneath his mighty hand.

Many towns would share this grief.

Their names contained meanings that pointed to the calamities approaching them.

The intention was to awaken a holy fear of God's wrath.

All refuges other than Jesus Christ become false shelters for people who place their ultimate trust in them.

Every earthly inheritance passes to later heirs, except the heavenly inheritance.

Every human glory will eventually become shame, except the honor that comes from God alone.

Sinners may now ignore the suffering of their neighbors.

But the time for their own judgment will also come.
classic_reading:
[Mic.1.1-Mic.1.7]
Micah
Micah was raised up to support Isaiah, and to confirm his predictions, while he invited to repentance, both by threatened judgments and promised mercies. A very remarkable passage, Mi 5 contains a summary of prophecies concerning the Messiah.
Chapter 1
Chapter Outline
The wrath of God against Israel. | (1-7) |
Also against Jerusalem and other cities, Their precautions vain. | (8-16) |
Verses 1-7
The earth is called upon, with all that are therein, to hear the prophet. God's holy temple will not protect false professors. Neither men of high degree, as the mountains, nor men of low degree, as the valleys, can secure themselves or the land from the judgments of God. If sin be found in God's people he will not spare them; and their sins are most provoking to him, for they are most reproaching. When we feel the smart of sin, it behoves us to seek what is the sin we smart for. Persons and places most exalted, are most exposed to spiritual diseases. The vices of leaders and rulers shall be surely and sorely punished. The punishment answers the sin. What they gave to idols, never shall prosper, nor do them any good. What is got by one lust, is wasted on another.
[Mic.1.8-Mic.1.16]
Verses 8-16
The prophet laments that Israel's case is desperate; but declare it not in Gath. Gratify not those that make merry with the sins or with the sorrows of God's Israel. Roll thyself in the dust, as mourners used to do; let every house in Jerusalem become a house of Aphrah, "a house of dust." When God makes the house dust it becomes us to humble ourselves to the dust under his mighty hand. Many places should share this mourning. The names have meanings which pointed out the miseries coming upon them; thereby to awaken the people to a holy fear of Divine wrath. All refuges but Christ, must be refuges of lies to those who trust in them; other heirs will succeed to every inheritance but that of heaven; and all glory will be turned into shame, except that honour which cometh from God only. Sinners may now disregard their neighbours' sufferings, yet their turn to be punished will some come.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe sins and desolations of Israel.1–5Their evil practices.6–11A promise of restoration.12–13
The people plan evil and exploit their neighbors (verses 1–5)

Woe to people who plan evil during the night and rise early to carry it out!

It is bad to hurt others through a sudden thought.

It is worse to act with deliberation and careful planning.

How important it is to use hours of solitude wisely!

When greed rules the heart, compassion disappears.

Once the heart is captured in that way, the hands soon practice violence and fraud.

People who are arrogant and complacent in prosperity are often the first to despair when adversity arrives.

Woe to those from whom God turns away!

Some of the most severe judgments are those that remove us from the fellowship of God's people or deprive us of the benefits of worship.

God's word rejected; the world cannot give rest (verses 6–11)

The people told God's prophets not to preach.

God would let their own wish become their punishment.

Why should a physician continue visiting a patient who refuses to be healed?

Those who silence faithful ministers and obstruct access to the means of grace are enemies not only of God but also of their country.

If people feel no reverence for God's word, what can restrain their conduct?

Sinners should not expect lasting peace in a land they have polluted with wickedness.

They would be forced to leave it, and it would become the instrument of their ruin.

This also teaches us about our present world.

Sin has corrupted it.

We should avoid sharing in its corruption.

This world was designed as a place to pass through, not our final possession.

It is our inn, not our home.

We have no lasting city here.

Let us rise and seek the enduring city above.

People determined to be deceived will find teachers willing to deceive them.

Ministers who promote self-indulgence through their teaching and example will appeal to such listeners.

The Lord opens a way for his people (verses 12–13)

These verses may refer to the captivity of Israel and Judah and their eventual return.

Henry also sees a prophecy of Jewish conversion to Christ.

The Lord would bring his people out of captivity and multiply them.

Jesus Christ would open their way to God by taking on human nature and, through the Holy Spirit, breaking Satan's chains within their hearts.

He leads his people, and they follow.

In his strength they overcome the spiritual enemies that would block their way to heaven.
classic_reading:
[Mic.2.1-Mic.2.5]
Chapter 2
Chapter Outline
The sins and desolations of Israel. | (1-5) |
Their evil practices. | (6-11) |
A promise of restoration. | (12-13) |
Verses 1-5
Woe to the people that devise evil during the night, and rise early to carry it into execution! It is bad to do mischief on a sudden thought, much worse to do it with design and forethought. It is of great moment to improve and employ hours of retirement and solitude in a proper manner. If covetousness reigns in the heart, compassion is banished; and when the heart is thus engaged, violence and fraud commonly occupy the hands. The most haughty and secure in prosperity, are commonly most ready to despair in adversity. Woe to those from whom God turns away! Those are the sorest calamities which cut us off from the congregation of the Lord, or cut us short in the enjoyment of its privileges.
[Mic.2.6-Mic.2.11]
Verses 6-11
Since they say, "Prophesy not," God will take them at their word, and their sin shall be their punishment. Let the physician no longer attend the patient that will not be healed. Those are enemies, not only to God, but to their country, who silence good ministers, and stop the means of grace. What bonds will hold those who have no reverence for God's word? Sinners cannot expect to rest in a land they have polluted. You shall not only be obliged to depart out of this land, but it shall destroy you. Apply this to our state in this present world. There is corruption in the world through lust, and we should keep at a distance from it. It is not our rest: it was designed for our passage, but not for our portion; our inn, but not our home; here we have no continuing city; let us therefore arise and depart, let us seek a continuing city above. Since they will be deceived, let them be deceived. Teachers who recommend self-indulgence by their doctrine and example, best suit such sinners.
[Mic.2.12-Mic.2.13]
Verses 12-13
These verses may refer to the captivity of Israel and Judah. But the passage is also a prophecy of the conversion of the Jews to Christ. The Lord would not only bring them from captivity, and multiply them, but the Lord Jesus would open their way to God, by taking upon him the nature of man, and by the work of his Spirit in their hearts, breaking the fetters of Satan. Thus he has gone before, and the people follow, breaking, in his strength, through the enemies that would stop their way to heaven.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe cruelty of the princes, and the falsehood of the prophets.1–8Their false security.9–12
Cruel rulers and dishonest prophets (verses 1–8)

People cannot expect to live wickedly and yet enjoy lasting prosperity.

They may experience the same kind of harm they have done to others.

How rarely do uncomfortable but wholesome truths reach the ears of those with high rank and public authority!

People who mislead others are preparing humiliation for themselves.

Micah possessed a burning love for God and for people's souls.

He cared deeply about God's glory, their salvation and the destruction caused by sin.

The difficulties he encountered did not drive him away from his calling.

His strength came not from himself, but because he was filled with the Spirit of the Lord.

People who act honestly can also act boldly.

Those who come to hear God's word should be willing to have their sins pointed out.

They should receive correction graciously and with gratitude.

The false confidence of leaders (verses 9–12)

Zion's walls are no reason to honor people who built them by shed blood and injustice.

Human sin does not accomplish God's righteousness.

Even acts that are outwardly useful become hateful to God and to people when they are done for dishonest profit.

Faith rests upon the Lord as the soul's foundation.

Presumption merely leans upon God as a support when it is convenient, attempting to make him serve private interests.

Claiming that the Lord dwells among us does not protect us from judgment when his presence has not restrained our evil conduct.

Micah announced that Zion would be plowed like a field because of its leaders' sin.

Henry says the prophecy was fulfilled at the destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans and remained evident in his own day.

The historical interpretation belongs to Henry.

When sacred places are polluted with sin, God may rightly bring them to ruin.
classic_reading:
[Mic.3.1-Mic.3.8]
Chapter 3
Chapter Outline
The cruelty of the princes, and the falsehood of the prophets. | (1-8) |
Their false security. | (9-12) |
Verses 1-8
Men cannot expect to do ill, and fare well; but to find that done to them which they did to others. How seldom do wholesome truths reach the ears of those in high stations or in authority! Those who deceive others are preparing confusion for their own faces. The prophet had ardent love to God and to the souls of men; deep concern for his glory and their salvation, and zeal against sin. The difficulties he met with did not drive him from his work. He had this strength; not from and of himself, but he was full of power by the Spirit of the Lord. Those who act honestly, may act boldly. And those who come to hear the word of God, must be willing to be told of their faults, must take it kindly, and be thankful.
[Mic.3.9-Mic.3.12]
Verses 9-12
Zion's walls owe no thanks to those that build them up with blood and iniquity. The sin of man works not the righteousness of God. Even when men do that which in itself is good, but do it for filthy lucre, it becomes abomination both to God and man. Faith rests in the Lord as the soul's foundation: presumption only leans upon the Lord as a prop, and would use him to serve a turn. If men's having the Lord among them will not keep them from doing evil, it never can secure them from suffering evil for so doing. See the doom of wicked Jacob; Therefore shall Zion for your sake be ploughed as a field. This was exactly fulfilled at the destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans, and is so at this day. If sacred places are polluted by sin, they will be wasted and ruined by the judgments of God.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe peace of the kingdom of Christ.1–8The judgments to come upon Jerusalem, but the final triumph of Israel.9–13
Peace in Christ's kingdom (verses 1–8)

The nations have not yet submitted to the Prince of Peace so fully that swords have become plowshares and warfare has ceased.

Yet these promises concerning the gospel church are precious.

They will increasingly be fulfilled because the One who promised is faithful.

In the latter days, during the reign of the Messiah, a glorious church will be established.

Christ himself will build it upon a rock.

The Gentiles once worshiped false gods.

But the people described here will hold firmly to the Lord, love him wholeheartedly and delight in obeying his will.

Those who limp in their spiritual walk are people who do not follow God's word faithfully.

The return of the captives from Babylon was a pledge of future healing, cleansing and prosperity for the church.

Christ's reign will continue until it reaches the everlasting kingdom of heaven.

We should encourage one another to attend God's appointed worship, learn his ways and obey them.

God's law must be written upon our hearts by his Spirit.

That transformation gives evidence of our share in the Redeemer's righteousness.

Jerusalem's distress and final triumph (verses 9–13)

Many nations would gather against Zion, intending to celebrate her defeat.

But they would not know that the Lord had brought them together like bundles of grain prepared for threshing.

Zion would receive strength to overcome them.

Henry says nothing in Jewish history up to his time fully corresponded to this prophecy.

He expected its fulfillment in a future event.

Whenever God assigns his people work to overcome opposition, he also provides the strength and ability they need.

Believers facing suffering should cry out in the prayer of faith, not in hopelessness.
classic_reading:
[Mic.4.1-Mic.4.8]
Chapter 4
Chapter Outline
The peace of the kingdom of Christ. | (1-8) |
The judgments to come upon Jerusalem, but the final triumph of Israel. | (9-13) |
Verses 1-8
The nations have not yet so submitted to the Prince of Peace, as to beat their swords into ploughshares, nor has war ceased. But very precious promises these are, relating to the gospel church, which will be more and more fulfilled, for He is faithful that has promised. There shall be a glorious church for God set up in the world, in the last days, in the days of the Messiah. Christ himself will build it upon a rock. The Gentiles worshipped their idol gods; but in the period spoken of, the people will cleave to the Lord with full purpose of heart, and delight in doing his will. The word "halteth," describes those who walk not according to the Divine word. The collecting the captives from Babylon was an earnest of healing, purifying, and prospering the church; and the reign of Christ shall continue till succeeded by the everlasting kingdom of heaven. Let us stir up each other to attend the ordinances of God, that we may learn his holy ways, and walk in them, receiving the law from his hands, which, being written in our hearts by his Spirit, may show our interest in the Redeemer's righteousness.
[Mic.4.9-Mic.4.13]
Verses 9-13
Many nations would assemble against Zion to rejoice in her calamities. They would not understand that the Lord had collected them as sheaves are gathered to be threshed; and that Zion would be strengthened to beat them to pieces. Nothing has yet taken place in the history of the Jewish church agreeing with this prediction. When God has conquering work for his people to do, he will furnish them with strength and ability for it. Believers should cry aloud under distresses, with the prayer of faith, not with despondency.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe birth of Christ and conversion of the Gentiles.1–6The triumphs of Israel.7–15
Christ's birth in Bethlehem and his kingdom (verses 1–6)

After announcing how greatly David's royal family would be brought low, Micah gave a promise about the Messiah and his kingdom to strengthen God's people's faith.

The prophecy reveals Christ's eternal existence as God and his work as Mediator.

His birth would take place in Bethlehem.

The Jews understood that location as the Messiah's birthplace (Matthew 2:5).

Christ's government brings happiness to his people.

They may enjoy security and rest under his care.

The promised protection from the Assyrians also represents the protection Christ gives the gospel church and individual believers against the powers of darkness.

Christ is our Peace as Priest, because he atones for sin and reconciles us to God.

Christ is our Peace as King, because he conquers our enemies.

Therefore our souls may rest confidently in him.

Christ will also provide human instruments of protection and deliverance.

Those who attempt to destroy God's church frequently bring destruction upon themselves.

Henry sees these promises as possibly encompassing the past successes of gospel preaching, the future spread of the gospel and the downfall of powers opposing Christ.

He calls this perhaps the most important single prophecy in the Old Testament, because it reveals the Messiah's personal character and the way he would be made known to the world.

It distinguishes his birth as a human being from his eternal divine existence.

Henry also understands it to predict Israel's temporary rejection and final restoration, and universal peace in the latter days.

Meanwhile, let us trust our Shepherd's care and power.

If he allows enemies to attack, he will provide the assistance we need.

The remnant of Israel and its victories (verses 7–15)

The remnant of Israel converted to Christ during the early Christian period was scattered among many nations like drops of dew.

These believers became instruments by which many additional people were brought into spiritual worship.

For people who rejected or opposed salvation, however, they became like lions.

Their message condemned those who persisted in unbelief.

God promised not only the reform of the Jews but also the purification of the Christian church.

Likewise, in our own spiritual struggles, we can expect victory when we depend simply upon the Lord our salvation, worship him and serve him diligently.
classic_reading:
[Mic.5.1-Mic.5.6]
Chapter 5
Chapter Outline
The birth of Christ and conversion of the Gentiles. | (1-6) |
The triumphs of Israel. | (7-15) |
Verses 1-6
Having showed how low the house of David would be brought, a prediction of the Messiah and his kingdom is added to encourage the faith of God's people. His existence from eternity as God, and his office as Mediator, are noticed. Here is foretold that Bethlehem should be his birthplace. Hence it was universally known among the Jews, [Matt.2.5] Mt 2:5. Christ's government shall be very happy for his subjects; they shall be safe and easy. Under the shadow of protection from the Assyrians, is a promise of protection to the gospel church and all believers, from the designs and attempts of the powers of darkness. Christ is our Peace as a Priest, making atonement for sin, and reconciling us to God; and he is our Peace as a King, conquering our enemies: hence our souls may dwell at ease in him. Christ will find instruments to protect and deliver. Those that threaten ruin to the church of God, soon bring ruin on themselves. This may include the past powerful effects of the preached gospel, its future spread, and the ruin of all antichristian powers. This is, perhaps, the most important single prophecy in the Old Testament: it respects the personal character of the Messiah, and the discoveries of himself to the world. It distinguishes his human birth from his existing from eternity; it foretells the rejection of the Israelites and Jews for a season, their final restoration, and the universal peace to prevail through the whole earth in the latter days. In the mean time let us trust our Shepherd's care and power. If he permits the assault of our enemies, he will supply helpers and assistance for us.
[Mic.5.7-Mic.5.15]
Verses 7-15
The remnant of Israel, converted to Christ in the primitive times, were among many nations as the drops of dew, and were made instruments in calling a large increase of spiritual worshippers. But to those who neglected or opposed this salvation, they would, as lions, cause terror, their doctrine condemning them. The Lord also declares that he would cause not only the reformation of the Jews, but the purification of the Christian church. In like manner shall we be assured of victory in our personal conflicts, as we simply depend upon the Lord our salvation, worship him, and serve him with diligence.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesGod's controversy with Israel.1–5The duties God requires.6–8The wickedness of Israel.9–16
God calls Israel to account (verses 1–5)

God called the people to explain why they were tired of his worship and inclined toward idolatry.

Sin creates the dispute between God and humanity.

The Lord reasons with us to teach us how to examine our own conduct honestly.

He called Israel to remember the many favors shown both to them and to their ancestors.

They should compare those gifts with their own ungrateful and shameful behavior.

What does God require? (verses 6–8)

Henry says these verses seem to reflect the substance of Balak's consultation with Balaam about how to obtain Israel's God's favor.

A deep awareness of guilt and judgment makes people ask urgently how to find pardon and peace.

That concern may be an early sign of hope.

But we must learn that acceptance with God rests upon the atoning work of Jesus Christ.

We must also leave the sins through which we offend him.

What could satisfy God's justice?

In whose name can we come, since we have no righteousness of our own to plead?

In what righteousness can we appear before him?

The sacrifices the people proposed were impressive and expensive.

Their eagerness showed some understanding of guilt, but they did not know the right means of pardon.

People deeply convinced of their sin and danger would surrender everything they owned if that would purchase forgiveness.

But their proposals could not succeed.

The animal sacrifices received their meaning from their reference to Christ.

It was impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to remove sin.

Every plan for peace with God outside the gospel fails.

No gift offered by sinners can satisfy divine justice or compensate for dishonoring God through sin.

Nor can offerings ever replace holiness of heart and a reformed life.

People may surrender almost anything except their sins.

Yet no offering makes them acceptable to God if they refuse to abandon their sins.

God commands moral duties because they are good for human beings.

Keeping his commandments brings reward in the keeping itself, as well as afterward.

God has made his requirements clear and understandable.

What he requires is not a payment for pardon, but love for him, expressed through doing justice, loving mercy and walking humbly with him.

Nothing in that is unreasonable.

If we are to walk happily with God, every thought must be brought into obedience to him.

We must do this as repentant sinners depending on the Redeemer and his atonement.

Blessed be God, who is ready to give grace to the humble person who waits for him.

Israel's injustice cannot be excused (verses 9–16)

God had made the duty to do justice clear.

The same passage now showed plainly how Israel had acted unjustly.

Hear the Lord's warning before the rod of judgment arrives.

And when correction does come, listen to its guidance.

God's voice should be heard in his acts of discipline.

People who are dishonest in business cannot be considered pure simply because they make a show of religious devotion.

What comes through fraud and oppression cannot be kept or enjoyed with genuine peace.

The possessions we cling to most tightly are often lost first.

Sin is a root of bitterness, easy to plant but difficult to remove.

It was once an honor for Israel to be called God's people.

But when they abandoned him, the name became a reproach rather than an honor.
classic_reading:
[Mic.6.1-Mic.6.5]
Chapter 6
Chapter Outline
God's controversy with Israel. | (1-5) |
The duties God requires. | (6-8) |
The wickedness of Israel. | (9-16) |
Verses 1-5
The people are called upon to declare why they were weary of God's worship, and prone to idolatry. Sin causes the controversy between God and man. God reasons with us, to teach us to reason with ourselves. Let them remember God's many favours to them and their fathers, and compare with them their unworthy, ungrateful conduct toward him.
[Mic.6.6-Mic.6.8]
Verses 6-8
These verses seem to contain the substance of Balak's consultation with Balaam how to obtain the favour of Israel's God. Deep conviction of guilt and wrath will put men upon careful inquiries after peace and pardon, and then there begins to be some ground for hope of them. In order to God's being pleased with us, our care must be for an interest in the atonement of Christ, and that the sin by which we displease him may be taken away. What will be a satisfaction to God's justice? In whose name must we come, as we have nothing to plead as our own? In what righteousness shall we appear before him? The proposals betray ignorance, though they show zeal. They offer that which is very rich and costly. Those who are fully convinced of sin, and of their misery and danger by reason of it, would give all the world, if they had it, for peace and pardon. Yet they do not offer aright. The sacrifices had value from their reference to Christ; it was impossible that the blood of bulls and goats should take away sin. And all proposals of peace, except those according to the gospel, are absurd. They could not answer the demands of Divine justice, nor satisfy the wrong done to the honour of God by sin, nor would they serve at all in place of holiness of the heart and reformation of the life. Men will part with any thing rather than their sins; but they part with nothing so as to be accepted of God, unless they do part with their sins. Moral duties are commanded because they are good for man. In keeping God's commandments there is a great reward, as well as after keeping them. God has not only made it known, but made it plain. The good which God requires of us is, not the paying a price for the pardon of sin and acceptance with God, but love to himself; and what is there unreasonable, or hard, in this? Every thought within us must be brought down, to be brought into obedience to God, if we would walk comfortably with him. We must do this as penitent sinners, in dependence on the Redeemer and his atonement. Blessed be the Lord that he is ever ready to give his grace to the humble, waiting penitent.
[Mic.6.9-Mic.6.16]
Verses 9-16
God, having showed how necessary it was that they should do justly, here shows how plain it was that they had done unjustly. This voice of the Lord says to all, Hear the rod when it is coming, before you see it, and feel it. Hear the rod when it is come, and you are sensible of the smart; hear what counsels, what cautions it speaks. The voice of God is to be heard in the rod of God. Those who are dishonest in their dealings shall never be reckoned pure, whatever shows of devotion they may make. What is got by fraud and oppression, cannot be kept or enjoyed with satisfaction. What we hold closest we commonly lose soonest. Sin is a root of bitterness, soon planted, but not soon plucked up again. Their being the people of God in name and profession, while they kept themselves in his love, was an honour to them; but now, being backsliders, their having been once the people of God turns to their reproach.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe general prevalence of wickedness.1–7Reliance on God, and triumph over enemies.8–13Promises and encouragements for Israel.14–20
Wickedness spreads even through families (verses 1–7)

The prophet grieved that he was living among people rapidly approaching judgment.

Many righteous people would suffer alongside them.

Even families and close relatives no longer brought comfort.

Neglect and contempt for family responsibilities are sad signs of widespread corruption.

People who refuse proper respect and service to their parents are unlikely to live well.

Micah found safety and consolation only in looking to the Lord and waiting for God his Savior.

During suffering, we should continually look to our divine Redeemer for faith and strength.

He will enable us to trust him and be good examples to those around us.

Trusting God while waiting for deliverance (verses 8–13)

People who have truly repented of sin find strong reasons to be patient under affliction.

When we complain to God about the wickedness of our age, we should also confess the sins of our own hearts.

We must rely on him to bring rescue at the proper time.

We should not only look to him but also look expectantly for him.

Even during our worst distress, we need not despair of salvation when we trust the Lord as the God of our salvation.

Enemies may celebrate our ruin, but eventually their pride will be silenced.

Zion's walls may lie broken for a long time, but a day will come when they are rebuilt.

Israel will return from distant places, without turning back because of discouragement.

When enemies seem to prevail, we should not become hopeless.

Though cast down, we are not destroyed.

We can combine hope in God's mercy with submission to his correction.

No obstacle can prevent the blessings the Lord has decided to give his church.

God's shepherding and complete forgiveness (verses 14–20)

When God is preparing to deliver his people, he moves their friends to pray for them.

Henry understands the prophet's prayer as applying spiritually to Christ, the great Shepherd of his sheep.

Christ leads and cares for his people while they travel through this world, where they are present but do not belong.

God's promise in answer to prayer is that he will act for them with power reminiscent of the miracles of earlier ages.

Sin brought the people into bondage.

God's forgiveness releases them from it.

Everyone who experiences pardoning mercy has reason to be amazed.

When the Lord removes the guilt of sin, so that it can no longer condemn us, he also breaks the ruling power of sin, so that it cannot continue to dominate us.

Our own strength is insufficient to defeat remaining sinful desires.

But God's grace is enough to subdue them.

If sin no longer rules us, it will not ruin us.

When God forgives, he ensures that the sin is no longer remembered against the sinner.

He throws the sins into the depths of the sea, not merely into shallow water near shore where they might reappear.

They will never rise again.

He casts all their sins into that depth, because when he pardons, he pardons completely.

The Lord will finish the work he began for us and do everything our condition needs according to his promises.

Henry connects these promises with Christ, the success of the gospel through the end of time, the future restoration of Israel and the final spread of true religion throughout the nations.

God will fulfill every part of his truth and mercy.

Nothing he promised will fail.

The One who made the promises is faithful and will accomplish them.

The security of his covenant gives strong consolation to everyone who flees to Christ for refuge and holds onto the hope set before them.
classic_reading:
[Mic.7.1-Mic.7.7]
Chapter 7
Chapter Outline
The general prevalence of wickedness. | (1-7) |
Reliance on God, and triumph over enemies. | (8-13) |
Promises and encouragements for Israel. | (14-20) |
Verses 1-7
The prophet bemoans himself that he lived among a people ripening apace for ruin, in which many good persons would suffer. Men had no comfort, no satisfaction in their own families or in their nearest relations. Contempt and violation of domestic duties are a sad symptom of universal corruption. Those are never likely to come to good who are undutiful to their parents. The prophet saw no safety or comfort but in looking to the Lord, and waiting on God his salvation. When under trials, we should look continually to our Divine Redeemer, that we may have strength and grace to trust in him, and to be examples to those around us.
[Mic.7.8-Mic.7.13]
Verses 8-13
Those truly penitent for sin, will see great reason to be patient under affliction. When we complain to the Lord of the badness of the times, we ought to complain against ourselves for the badness of our hearts. We must depend upon God to work deliverance for us in due time. We must not only look to him, but look for him. In our greatest distresses, we shall see no reason to despair of salvation, if by faith we look to the Lord as the God of our salvation. Though enemies triumph and insult, they shall be silenced and put to shame. Though Zion's walls may long be in ruins, there will come a day when they shall be repaired. Israel shall come from all the remote parts, not turning back for discouragements. Though our enemies may seem to prevail against us, and to rejoice over us, we should not despond. Though cast down, we are not destroyed; we may join hope in God's mercy, with submission to his correction. No hinderances can prevent the favours the Lord intends for his church.
[Mic.7.14-Mic.7.20]
Verses 14-20
When God is about to deliver his people, he stirs up their friends to pray for them. Apply spiritually the prophet's prayer to Christ, to take care of his church, as the great Shepherd of the sheep, and to go before them, while they are here in this world as in a wood, in this world but not of it. God promises in answer to this prayer, he will do that for them which shall be repeating the miracles of former ages. As their sin brought them into bondage, so God's pardoning their sin brought them out. All who find pardoning mercy, cannot but wonder at that mercy; we have reason to stand amazed, if we know what it is. When the Lord takes away the guilt of sin, that it may not condemn us, he will break the power of sin, that it may not have dominion over us. If left to ourselves, our sins will be too hard for us; but God's grace shall be sufficient to subdue them, so that they shall not rule us, and then they shall not ruin us. When God forgives sin, he takes care that it never shall be remembered any more against the sinner. He casts their sins into the sea; not near the shore-side, where they may appear again, but into the depth of the sea, never to rise again. All their sins shall be cast there, for when God forgives sin, he forgives all. He will perfect that which concerns us, and with this good work will do all for us which our case requires, and which he has promised. These engagements relate to Christ, and the success of the gospel to the end of time, the future restoration of Israel, and the final prevailing of true religion in all lands. The Lord will perform his truth and mercy, not one jot or tittle of it shall fall to the ground: faithful is He that has promised, who also will do it. Let us remember that the Lord has given the security of his covenant, for strong consolation to all who flee for refuge to lay hold on the hope set before them in Christ Jesus.
